full_story_part1.text: Are people who earn more always more hardworking? When people discuss income and personality, they often look for things successful people have in common. But this time, let's ask the high earner next door to step away from the stage for a moment. The person in the spotlight is none other than you. The research team gathered information from 11 studies and studied it. The studies followed the same people over time. The people in them had jobs. They reported their personalities and income from work. Researchers asked about both at least 3 times. So this was not one picture, but a set of pictures showing changes over time.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
“Are people who earn more always more hardworking?” When people discuss income and personality, they often look for “things successful people have in common.” But this time, let’s ask the high earner next door to step away from the stage for a moment. The person in the spotlight is none other than you.

The research team gathered information from 11 studies and studied it. The studies followed the same people over time. The people in them had jobs. They reported their personalities and income from work. Researchers asked about both at least three times. So this was not one picture, but a set of pictures showing changes over time.

full_story_part2.text: The way researchers looked at the data matters. They separated differences between people from changes within one person. One example is. That person works harder than I do and earns more. Another question is. How did my personality change after my income changed? They moved from ranking people by yearly income to following one person over time. It was a different contest altogether. The trait they focused on was conscientiousness. the habit of working seriously and steadily. Their study found that, within the same person, higher income was linked to greater conscientiousness later on. Wait—we thought personality affected income. But income had a part too! But the arrow does not point only one way. A rise in conscientiousness was also weakly linked to higher income later. They found a weak link in both directions. personality with later income, and income with later personality.

It was a different contest altogether.

The trait they focused on was conscientiousness: the habit of working seriously and steadily. Their study found that, within the same person, higher income was linked to greater conscientiousness later on.

Wait—we thought personality affected income. But income had a part too!

But the arrow does not point only one way. A rise in conscientiousness was also weakly linked to higher income later. They found a weak link in both directions: personality with later income, and income with later personality.

full_story_part3.text: After hearing this, you may want to ask, Does a pay raise change your personality too? But wait before you decide that is true. The team studied data that tracked changes over time. This cannot prove that income changed personality, or that personality increased income. Something else may have affected both. Coming first and being the cause are 2 different things. In a drama, the person we see first at the scene is not always the criminal. The order of events can give us a clue, but it cannot solve the case by itself. So when you look back at your income or the way you work, you do not have to end with, That's just my personality. Ask instead, What has changed in me lately? Then look more closely. Instead of judging other people, look for changes in yourself. With income and personality, changing who you compare yourself with can show a very different picture.

After hearing this, you may want to ask, “Does a pay raise change your personality too?” But wait before you decide that is true. The team studied data that tracked changes over time. This cannot prove that income changed personality, or that personality increased income. Something else may have affected both.

“Coming first” and “being the cause” are two different things. In a drama, the person we see first at the scene is not always the criminal. The order of events can give us a clue, but it cannot solve the case by itself.

So when you look back at your income or the way you work, you do not have to end with, “That’s just my personality.” Ask instead, “What has changed in me lately?” Then look more closely. Instead of judging other people, look for changes in yourself. With income and personality, changing who you compare yourself with can show a very different picture.
